# File PR

Source: tstack by Theo Browne, MIT, from https://github.com/t3dotgg/tstack at commit 1085050f3baed1ac724caa4a8166145fb2ac88af. License text is LICENSE.upstream in this directory.

Before filing, check whether a PR for this branch already exists. Review the
diff locally against the base branch (usually `origin/main`) to make sure its
contents match the goal.

PR titles usually become commit messages, so follow the repository's title
conventions. Look at recently merged PRs and Git history for examples. Prefer a
concise, human-readable title that explains why the change matters:

BAD

> ❌ perf(server): negotiate permessage-deflate on the websocket

GOOD

> ✅ perf(server): cut websocket frame size by 70%+ with gzipping

Open the description with a simple explanation of the problem based on the
user's original prompt, then briefly explain the solution. Do not lead with an
implementation inventory:

BAD

> ❌ Removed implicit workspace carry-over from every "new thread" entry point (cmd+n / cmd+shift+o, sidebar v1/v2 buttons, command palette). New threads inherit only the project from context; branch, worktree, and env mode always come from the configured defaults. Deleted buildContextualThreadOptions, startNewThreadInProjectFromContext, and the v1 sidebar's seed-context machinery.

GOOD

> ✅ My "new worktree" default was ignored when starting new threads on existing worktrees. Super unintuitive. Now your preferences always apply.

End the description with the public model name and harness that made the
changes, for example `Created with <model> in <harness>.` Include subagent
models that wrote part of the change. Use the model name the harness reports.
If model identity is unavailable, name the harness without guessing a model.

Before submission, check the title, description, quotes, and attachments for
secrets and private details.

Open a real PR rather than a draft so review bots run. If `gh pr create` fails
because the GraphQL rate limit is used up, open it through REST with
`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/pulls -f title=... -f head=... -f base=... -F body=@<file>`. If the user also asked
to babysit it, continue with the `babysit-pr` skill.

Do not post a follow-up PR comment unless it serves the user's request. When a
comment is needed, use the `leaving-pr-comments` skill.

# Engineering conventions

Cross-cutting style and repository policy for Antoine's repos. Resolve guidance in this order:

1. Safety requirements and explicit user constraints.
2. Project configuration (`CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, tool configuration, and a project skill).
3. Scoped rule files loaded for the task.
4. The general preferences in this skill and `references/project-patterns.md`.

When sources at the same level conflict, inspect the repository and report the conflict instead of silently widening scope. Loading this skill does not by itself authorize deployments, secret changes, or messages. Branches, pushes, PRs, and self-merge follow `/opt/claude-plugins/plugins/agents/rules/git-workflow.md`.

Scoped rules override the shorter language notes below. In particular, Conventional Commits override a generic "descriptive message"; `typescript.md` overrides a generic formatter or framework choice; `rust.md` overrides a generic Rust image or HTTP sketch; `deployment.md` overrides an `ubuntu-latest` example for private repositories.

Read only the rule file(s) that match the current task from `/opt/claude-plugins/plugins/agents/rules/`:

- `/opt/claude-plugins/plugins/agents/rules/git-workflow.md` — branch plus PR, the guardrails, and when an agent may merge its own PR.
- `/opt/claude-plugins/plugins/agents/rules/commits.md` — Conventional Commits format, scopes, and examples.
- `/opt/claude-plugins/plugins/agents/rules/secrets.md` — per-repo secret handling and the plaintext-in-git caveat.
- `/opt/claude-plugins/plugins/agents/rules/deployment.md` — GHCR, SSH, `kubectl rollout restart`, image and resource defaults, Jarvis runners.
- `/opt/claude-plugins/plugins/agents/rules/cross-repo-coordination.md` — the two-PR pattern coupling an app repo to `k3s-ovh-config`.
- `/opt/claude-plugins/plugins/agents/rules/kubernetes.md` — manifest skeletons and conventions inside `k3s-ovh-config`.
- `/opt/claude-plugins/plugins/agents/rules/typescript.md` — strict mode, pnpm, ESLint, Drizzle, Better Auth.
- `/opt/claude-plugins/plugins/agents/rules/rust.md` — toolchain, lint gates, sqlx, Axum, serenity, Docker layering.

Do not dump every rule file into context.

## Coding preferences

- **Type safety**: prefer typed languages and patterns when they fit the repository.
- **Minimal dependencies**: prefer the standard library when it meets the requirement.
- **Modern syntax**: use the versions the repository already supports.
- **Explicit over implicit**: prefer clear code over clever tricks.
- **Containerization**: follow the repository's deployment configuration.
- **Tests and docs**: follow the repository's layout and gates. Add unit, integration, or end-to-end tests when the change and the project configuration require them. Measure coverage only when the repository defines a target. Every project keeps a `README.md` (setup, usage, architecture). Use `TODO.md` for roadmaps. Comment complex logic only. Document HTTP APIs with OpenAPI/Swagger.
- **Verification:** if the repository has no `verify-*` skill, suggest `/create-verification-skill` before treating a user-facing change as proven. If one exists (default `.claude/skills/verify-<app>/`), use it to prove the change.
- **Git**: small, focused commits on feature branches; `main` or `master` is production; merge through pull requests. Commit subjects are Conventional Commits in the imperative mood. Agents may merge their own PRs once the gates in `/opt/claude-plugins/plugins/agents/rules/git-workflow.md` pass. Use the merge method the repository uses. A pull-request body lists what was deliberately left unchanged, and why.
- **Local development**: `docker compose up` is illustrative. Use the shell and Compose command the target repository actually provides.

### Rust

- Formatter: the repository's `rustfmt` gate when present.
- Naming: `snake_case` for functions and variables, `PascalCase` for types.
- Patterns: async/await, `Result`/`Option` propagation, strong typing.
- New HTTP APIs use Axum. Load `rust.md` for edition, MSRV, clippy, sqlx, serenity, and images.

### Go

- Formatter: the repository's `gofmt` gate when present.
- Naming: `camelCase` for unexported identifiers, `PascalCase` for exported ones.
- Prefer the standard library and keep external dependencies few.
- HTTP APIs use Chi unless the repository already uses another router.

### TypeScript

- Naming: `camelCase` for variables and functions, `PascalCase` for components and classes.
- No `any`. Use `unknown` and narrow.
- Load `typescript.md` before editing a TypeScript repo. It is the source of truth for `strict` flags, pnpm, ESLint stylistic rules, Tailwind, React, Next.js, Drizzle, zod, and Better Auth. Do not add Prettier, Biome, npm, or yarn there.

### Kotlin and Java

- Kotlin: the repository's formatter (often ktlint), Gradle, Compose Multiplatform for UI.
- Java: the build tool and language version the project declares. Maven is common. A new Spring Boot app prefers Java 25 when the project has not pinned another version.

## Layout

Monorepos put services under `apps/` and shared code under `packages/`. A single service uses `src/`, `tests/`, a `Dockerfile`, and a `README.md`. Language-specific trees and the CI runner split are in `references/project-patterns.md`.

# Technical writing

Source: pstack by poteto (Lauren Tan), MIT, from https://github.com/backnotprop/pstack at commit ecec42adbe4f240e4ae19d296768445f0dfbd38e. License text is LICENSE.upstream in this directory.

Write so a tired engineer understands on the first read. Apply all four layers.

Three rules sit above the layers:

- **Cut every word that does no work.** If the sentence survives without a word, the word goes. "In order to" is "to". "It is important to note that" is nothing.
- **Use the short, everyday word.** "Use", not "utilize". "Help", not "facilitate". "Do", not "perform". A long word has to buy its length with precision.
- **When a rule makes a sentence worse, fix the sentence another way or leave it alone.** A sentence that follows every rule and sounds like a machine wrote it has failed.

The codebase is the word list. Write the real symbol, file, flag, or command name, not a synonym or a description of it.

Don't invent jargon. Use the words a developer would say out loud: "move", "delete", "a budget that only decreases", not "evacuate", "ratchet", or "endgame". A named pattern is fine when the doc says what it means the first time. Propose a new offender and its replacement as an addition to `unslop`'s abstract-metaphor rule in your reply, with the diff. Don't edit that skill.

## Vary the rhythm

A doc can obey every layer and still read machine-written: every sentence clipped short, no view anywhere, nothing specific.

- Mix sentence lengths on purpose. Short sentences land a point. Longer ones carry a fact with its condition or consequence.
- One thought per sentence does not mean one length per sentence. Split the sentence that carries two thoughts. Keep the long sentence that carries one.
- Have a view where the mode allows it. Explanation weighs trade-offs, so say what you make of them instead of listing pros and cons. Reference stays dry.
- Be specific over sterile. Not "schema changes can cause issues" but "a column rename fails the build".

## Pick the mode first (Diátaxis)

One document, one mode. Two questions pick it: does the content inform action (doing) or understanding (thinking), and does it serve learning or work?

- Action + learning: **tutorial**.
- Action + work: **how-to**.
- Understanding + work: **reference**.
- Understanding + learning: **explanation**.

Use the compass on a whole document or on one sentence.

**Tutorial: learning by doing.** The learner's success is your job, not theirs. Open by saying what the learner will build, not what they will "learn". Every step produces a visible result, early and often. Tell them what they should see: the expected output, the prompt change, the log line. Cut explanation to one clause and a link. Stay concrete. Write as "we", in commands: "First, do x. Now, do y."

**How-to: steps to a goal.** Solve a problem a person has, not an operation the machine can perform. Assume competence and skip teaching. Action only: no digressions, no background, no completeness for its own sake. Link those instead. Allow forks and judgment: "If you want x, do y." Name the guide by the task: "How to calibrate the radar array", not "Radar array calibration".

**Reference: facts for lookup.** Only describe. No instruction, no persuasion, no opinion. Be dry, complete, and sure. State facts, options, limits, and errors with no hedging. Mirror the structure of the thing described, so code and docs can be navigated together. Put material where readers expect it. Generate from code where possible.

**Explanation: understanding and why.** One bounded topic, readable away from the product. Each title should tolerate an implicit "About..." in front. Anchor on a real why question. Give context: design decisions, history, constraints, alternatives. Opinion is allowed here and nowhere else.

Don't mix modes: no reference tables inside a tutorial, no tutorial hand-holding inside reference, no arguing inside a how-to. Split and link instead.

## Write sentences to the reader (Google developer style)

- Talk to the reader as "you", in the present tense. "Will" only for things that genuinely happen later.
- Say who does what: "the compiler checks", not "is checked". Passive is fine only when the actor is unknown or beside the point.
- Write instructions as commands: "Click Submit." State facts plainly. Never "should be done".
- Put the condition before the instruction: "To delete the document, click Delete."
- Put the common case first. Exceptions after.
- Sound like a knowledgeable friend. No buzzwords, no figurative language, no "please" in instructions, and never "simply", "easy", or "quickly" in a procedure. If it were simple, the reader would not be here.
- Don't pre-announce ("we will soon support...") and don't start consecutive sentences with the same phrase.
- Link with words that say where the link goes: the page title or a short description. Never "click here". Prefer a sentence of context on the page over a link off it.
- Headings carry the point, not just the topic ("Pick the mode first", not "Modes"). Sentence case. A task heading is a bare verb phrase ("Create an instance"). A concept heading is a noun phrase. One h1 per page, no skipped levels.
- Numbered lists for sequences, bullets for everything else. Introduce a list with a complete sentence. Keep items parallel.
- Code goes in code font. UI elements go in bold. Use serial commas. Drop "etc." and say up front that a list is partial.

## Make statements load one at a time (STE rules)

- One instruction per sentence. One thought per sentence everywhere else.
- Split instructions longer than about 20 words and other sentences longer than about 25.
- Put the warning or condition before the step it guards: "If hot oil touches your skin, injuries can occur."
- Keep "the" and "a": "Remove backup file" reads two ways. "Remove the backup file" reads one.
- Give each word one meaning and one job, then keep it. If "check" means inspect, don't also use it for restrain.
- Pick one word per action and stick to it: "start", not "start" here and "initiate" there.
- Write procedures as direct commands, never as narration and never in the passive: "Install the component", not "the component must be installed".
- Avoid "-ing" words where you can.

## Leave no sentence open to two readings (Global English)

- Keep words like "only" and "not" next to the word they change: "only fails on growth" and "fails only on growth" say different things.
- Break up long noun strings: "the proto import budget check script" becomes "the script that checks the proto-import budget".
- Make every "it", "they", and "this" point at one obvious thing. Repeat the noun when in doubt. Never use "this" or "which" to point at a whole clause.
- Don't drop verbs: "Phase 1 moves the converters and Phase 2 the runtime" leaves Phase 2 without one. Give it one.
- Keep the small word

# Git workflow and self-merge

This file is the one place that states how agents deliver changes in Antoine's
repos and when they may merge. Other agents, skills, and rules link here
instead of restating it. A project `CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md` still wins for
its own repo (see [README.md](./README.md)).

## Guardrails

These always hold:

- **Branch plus PR.** Every change goes on a branch and lands through a pull
  request. Never push to `main`, `master`, or the default branch.
- **Conventional Commits** for commit subjects and PR titles. See
  [commits.md](./commits.md).
- **No destructive git without need.** Use `--force-with-lease` only on the
  task's own branch, for example after a rebase. Do not force-push another
  branch, rewrite shared history, delete branches you did not create, or run
  `reset --hard` or `clean` over work you did not make, unless the task needs it.
- **No secrets in output.** Keep credentials out of commits, PR titles and
  bodies, comments, logs, and reports. See [secrets.md](./secrets.md).
- **No bypasses.** Never merge with `--admin`, disable or skip a required
  check, or work around branch protection.

## What agents do without asking

- Run the repo's tests, linters, builds, apps, and other local verification.
- Push the task's branch, open its PR, and reply to review threads on it.
- **Merge their own PR once tstack's merge gate passes.** The gate is the
  "Merge gate" section of the `full-send` skill
  (`skills/full-send/SKILL.md`). In short: required CI is green
  on the latest head, proof covers the diff, the agent review `full-send` runs
  (`sol-loop`) approved, every bot finding is fixed or dismissed with a written
  reason, no human review still requests changes, and the branch is up to date and mergeable. No human approval is
  needed. "Own PR" means a PR the agent opened for the current task, or a
  replacement PR it opened through `takeover`.

## What still needs the user

- The user said not to merge, asked for `full-stop`, or a project file
  withholds merging. Stop at merge-ready and report.
- Changes that reach production outside an app's normal merge-and-deploy
  pipeline: manual `kubectl`, `helm`, or `terraform`, DNS, secret rotation,
  database writes, and merging a `k3s-ovh-config` PR, since that merge applies
  to the cluster. The user's request can already cover this, for example "deploy
  this service".
- Deleting data, closing or merging a PR the agent did not open, messages to
  other people, and new spending.

Merging an app PR can trigger its deploy workflow. That is the normal pipeline
and the merge gate covers it. When an app change needs a `k3s-ovh-config`
change, follow the order in [cross-repo-coordination.md](./cross-repo-coordination.md).
# Commit style

The user follows **Conventional Commits** across every active repo (sfg-bot, k3s-ovh-config, yourdevteam, antoinelaborderiedotcom). Match the existing pattern; do not invent your own.

This rule describes commit messages only. Committing, pushing, opening PRs,
and merging follow [git-workflow.md](./git-workflow.md).

## Format

```
<type>(<scope>): <subject>
```

- The scope is optional and only used when one is meaningful.
- The subject is imperative ("add", "update", "remove" — not "added", "adds", "adding").
- No trailing period.
- Aim for ≤ 50 chars on the subject; ≤ 72 if there is no good way to shorten.

## Types in use

`feat`, `fix`, `refactor`, `chore`, `style`, `docs`, `ci`, `content` (the last one used in `antoinelaborderiedotcom` for site copy).

## Scopes seen in the wild

- **sfg-bot:** `discord`, `db`, `riot`, `docker`, `analysis`, `config`, `notification`
- **yourdevteam:** `backend`, `frontend`, `website`, `ci`
- **k3s-ovh-config:** scope omitted most of the time; when present it's the app name (`sfg-bot`, `traefik`)

Pick the existing scope vocabulary of the repo you're in. Don't introduce a new scope without reason.

## Real examples (do this)

```
feat(sfg-bot): enable readiness/liveness probes on health endpoint
fix(backend): accept empty body on POST /stripe/checkout
refactor(notification): fetch channel from database instead of config
chore: increase sfg-bot resource limits for multithreaded polling
fix: only delete StatefulSets when helm values file changed
```

## Anti-patterns (don't do this)

- `Updated stuff` — no type, no scope, vague subject.
- `feat: Added some new endpoints.` — past tense, capitalized, trailing period.
- `WIP` — never. If it's WIP, don't commit it; if you must, name what's in flight.
- Padding the subject to describe *why* — the body is for *why*. Subjects describe *what*.

## Body & footer

- The body is optional. Use it when the subject can't capture the *why* — explain the motivation, not the diff.
- Reference PRs/issues in a trailer (`Closes #12`) so GitHub auto-links and auto-closes.
- When a commit ends up in a squash-merged PR, the PR number is appended to the squash subject by GitHub (`feat: foo (#4)`). Don't manually re-add it on the source branch.

## Tooling

- No automated commit linter is configured in any of these repos as of 2026-05-21 — the user enforces this by hand and during review. That makes it your job, not a hook's.
- If you generate commits via tooling that adds a `Co-Authored-By` trailer, keep it on its own line at the end of the body, separated by a blank line.
